title: The first continents
summary: A study of the Singhbhum Craton in India proposes that thickening of the crust by magma, without plate tectonics, raised Earth's first continents above the sea 3.3 to 3.2 billion years ago. Sandstones there formed in rivers and shallow seas, and would once have formed some of the world's first beaches. Rocks of similar age occur in Australia and South Africa.

uncertainty.note: Detrital zircon U-Pb dating and sedimentary facies analysis date the subaerial emergence of the Singhbhum and related cratons to 3.3–3.0 Ga.

as_recorded.value: first continents 3.3 to 3.2 billion years ago

where.modern_name: No single place; stand-in pin in West Singhbhum, India
where.historical_name: Singhbhum Craton, Paleoarchean subaerial crust; no modern polities or geographical entities existed

paleo.not_applicable: Paleoarchean subaerial continental emergence across multiple proto-cratons prior to modern supercontinent cycles.

importance.justification: The subaerial emergence of Earth's first continents established terrestrial river systems, continental chemical weathering, and critical nutrient fluxes into Archean oceans.
